newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Red hot Beijing Enterprises set for cooling period.
newsitem.headline: Red hot Beijing Enterprises set for cooling period.

text.p: Beijing Enterprises Holdings Ltd's steaming entry onto the Hong Kong stock market should be followed by a cooling-off period over the short term but bumper gains still lie ahead, analysts said on Friday.

"The surge from the issue price has created quite a handsome profit for investors and that has stimulated strong profit-taking in the near run," said Ricky Tam, senior research manager at Delta Asia Securities.

"The stock is likely to consolidate between HK$38 and HK$45 (US$4.91 and US$5.81) in the short run before gaining sufficient momentum to rise further. It would not be surprising to see it rise to HK$50 or even HK$60 in the future," Tam added.

Beijing Enterprises stormed onto the Hong Kong market on Thursday, with its shares more than tripling in price on their stock market debut to HK$40.20 from an initial public offering price of HK$12.48.
The shares gained a further HK$5.00 on Friday to close at HK$45.20, bringing their price to earnings (P/E) multiple to about 67 times 1997 earnings, analysts said.

Other red chips, or Hong Kong-incorporated companies with financial backing from China, are trading at about 25-30 times earnings while blue-chip stocks are trading at a P/E multiple of about 14-15 times.
"The stock will trade around HK$45 to HK$48 in the short term," said Peter Lai, associate director at OCBC Securities.

The lucky investors who were alloted shares in the massively oversubscribed offering would be tempted to lock in their hefty gains over coming days, while those who were left out would be seeking to buy at around HK$40, analysts said.
Demand from overseas investors and institutions who had been unable to get in on the offering should also support the share price in the longer term, analysts said.
"You'll definitely see some buying around the HK$40 level," said Henry Lui, research analyst at Mansion House Research.
Lan Xue, associate director of SocGen-Crosby Securities, said the issue price of HK$12.48 fixed for the stock had been appropriate considering the company's underlying businesses.
"It's issue price of HK$12.48 is 20 times 1997 earnings, which is not particularly low," she said.
But the current P/E could prompt some investors to switch into some lagging red chip stocks, analysts said.
"The stock is overpriced at the current level," said Hugo So, an analyst at Yamaichi International.
A huge HK$200 million in interest income from subscription monies should take the P/E multiple lower and future asset injections would also boost future earnings, analysts said.
Beijing Enterprises' valuable connections to the Chinese capital have been a main driving force behind the stock's stunning market performance.
The conglomerate is controlled by the Beijing municipal government, which is expected to help Beijing Enterprises expand its businesses.
The company already owns a stake in Beijing McDonalds, the company which operates the fast-food chain in the city. It also has interests in brewing, toll roads, hotels and retailing.
"People are really thinking of the company's future rather than its current earnings," said Xue.
"It is very possible that the share price edges up to HK$50 to HK$60 by the end of the year due to asset injections," she added.
